taxonomyNote: Sources place this species in Masticophis (Nicholson 2025 via NatureServe) rather than Coluber; CWHR uses Coluber lateralis and notes it was formerly called California whipsnake.
fieldMarks: Slender, diurnal snake; a yellow stripe runs along each side (1 and 2 half scales wide in the Alameda form), hence 'striped racer' (NPS, Alameda subspecies).
Underside of the head may carry sparse speckled spots, or none; underside shades from cream to pink toward the tail; these features separate the Alameda form from other California whipsnakes (NPS).
behavior: Strictly diurnal and actively foraging on the surface, occasionally climbing shrubs or small trees; active March-November in California and non-migratory.
Preys mainly on lizards, also frogs, snakes, nestling birds, rodents and insects, hunting by sight and scent; shelters under objects, in crevices and rodent burrows.
Males are trapped more than females in spring because they roam widely for mates.
habitat: Chaparral, coastal scrub, shrubland with grassy patches, rocky canyons and watercourses, and woodland; prefers open-canopy stands with woody debris and rock outcrops on south-facing slopes.
range: California from the Sierra Nevada and Coast Ranges through southwestern California to northwestern Baja California; up to about 1,835 m in California. The Alameda striped racer subspecies is restricted to the Coast Ranges east of San Francisco Bay. Not in Canada.
